explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." (Psalm 23:1) "Not want" means he won't be missing what he needs. Picture a cookie jar that somehow never runs empty. I'd stop worrying about the grocery list too.

Close, friend, but David isn't talking about wages. He says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." (Psalm 23:1) The line is about what David has because of his shepherd. It's not about a paycheck. Nobody punches a time clock in this psalm.

I see why that sounds right, baker, because losing and wanting feel like neighbors. But David's word is about wanting: "I shall not want." (Psalm 23:1) He's saying he won't lack what he needs because the LORD is his shepherd. I once lost a whole afternoon looking for my own hat, and it was ON my head.

Yes, baker. David says, "He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters." (Psalm 23:2) Lying down and quiet water both say slow and calm. It's the feeling of a cookie sheet cooling on the rack, with nobody asking it for anything.

Not quite, friend. In this picture David is lying down: "He makes me lie down in green pastures." (Psalm 23:2) Nobody lies down in the middle of a hustle. Even my busiest day at the bakery has a moment where I sit and stare at the oven.

I get it, baker, because a song can turn dark fast. But this part stays calm: "He leads me beside quiet waters." (Psalm 23:2) Quiet waters and green pastures aren't the picture of a threat. The scary stuff shows up later in verse 4, so hold that thought.

That's right, friend. David says, "He restores my soul." (Psalm 23:3) The care isn't only for the outside, like grass and water. It reaches deep into David himself. Honestly, I know what restored feels like. I went from a dusty drawer to a brand new bakery, and my edges sharpened right up.
Nope, baker, but I see the thinking. Testing sounds serious and deep, like a soul thing. The text says, "He restores my soul." (Psalm 23:3) David is describing care, not a pop quiz.
Funny pick, friend. It sounds like a kitchen scale for souls. But David says, "He restores my soul." (Psalm 23:3) The word is restores, so the picture is soul care, not measuring.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. David says, "He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name." (Psalm 23:3) That's the reason David gives, and I won't add one the song doesn't. It points to the LORD's own name.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: That's a sweet guess, friend, and it fits a shepherd. But David's reason is different: "for the sake of His name." (Psalm 23:3) Flock is a word I'd expect, and the song doesn't use it there. Read the verse close and the answer is sitting right in it.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: Good try, baker, but there's no land in this verse. David says the LORD guides him "in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name." (Psalm 23:3) The reason is His name. I'd check a map and I still wouldn't find land in verse 3.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. David says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." (Psalm 23:4) The reason he gives is that the LORD is with him. It's not about the valley getting brighter. It's about who is walking beside him.

Not this time, baker. David's reason isn't his own muscle. He says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." (Psalm 23:4) He's counting on the LORD's company, not on going it alone. I tried going it alone in that junk drawer once, and all I got was a nap.

I see the logic, friend, since a short trip is easier to face. But the verse never says how long the valley is. David says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." (Psalm 23:4) His reason is that the LORD is with him.

True, baker. David says, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me." (Psalm 23:4) A big stick in a dark place sounds like trouble, but David calls it comfort. I think that tells you a lot about whose stick it is.

Careful, friend, this one is True. David says, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me." (Psalm 23:4) A rod and staff might sound scary by themselves. In this verse they're comfort, right there in the valley.

Yes, baker. David says, "You prepare a table before me." (Psalm 23:5) When somebody sets a table for you, you're a guest, and that's the picture. I love a good table. Mine usually has a cookie box on it.

Good thinking, friend, since shepherds live outdoors. But David's word is table: "You prepare a table before me." (Psalm 23:5) The picture here is a host and a guest. No tent in this verse, so no stakes to hammer.
I can see it, baker, since earlier David was lying down. But in verse 5 he says, "You prepare a table before me." (Psalm 23:5) The picture has changed to a host welcoming a guest. A table, not a bed.

Almost, baker, but this one is False. David says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." (Psalm 23:5) The word is "in the presence of," so his enemies are there. Far away would be a quieter dinner, but that's not what the verse says.

Right, friend. The text says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." (Psalm 23:5) It doesn't say far away. Enemies are in the room, and the table is still set. Now THAT is a dinner I'd want to hear about.

That's it, baker. David says, "my cup overflows." (Psalm 23:5) A cup that spills over holds more than it needs to. I think it's the same feeling as a batch that makes more cookies than the box can hold.

I get the thought, friend, since spilling can mean a mess. But nothing in the verse says David did something careless. He says, "my cup overflows," right after the LORD anoints his head with oil. (Psalm 23:5) I think the picture is of a cup filled past full.

Nice try, baker. But the verse doesn't say anyone is hurrying David. He's at a table the LORD prepared, and he says, "my cup overflows." (Psalm 23:5) I think an overflowing cup is about having plenty, not about being in a hurry.

You got it, baker. David says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." (Psalm 23:6) Something is following him, and it's goodness and mercy. That's a better tail than the dust bunnies I had.

Fair guess, friend, since David was a king. But his song names something else: "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." (Psalm 23:6) Wealth and honor don't show up in this verse. Goodness and mercy do.

Those sound great, baker, but they're not in David's line. He says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." (Psalm 23:6) It's goodness and mercy doing the following. Strength and wisdom would be good company too, but they didn't make this verse.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. David ends with, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever." (Psalm 23:6) The song that began with a shepherd ends at the LORD's house. I'd say that's a good place to land.

Interesting pick, baker, but Hebron isn't in this song. David closes with, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever." (Psalm 23:6) The word that matters is forever, and the place is the LORD's house.

That's a real place, friend, but it isn't what David names here. He ends with, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever." (Psalm 23:6) His last line points to the LORD's house, and it says forever. No map needed.
